extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, breeders, and students of natural history/evolution
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and lines of evidence used to evaluate the origin of domestic races and the action of selection (with pigeons as a focal example). Includes how to infer common ancestry, reversion, fertility, and the role of artificial and unconscious selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age-specific inheritance rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is no apparent reason why a peculiarity should appear at any particular age, it tends to appear in the offspring at the same period at which it first appeared in the parent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin regards this rule as of the highest importance in explaining embryology. Remark: confined to first appearance of the peculiarity, not its primary cause (which may act on ovules or male element). Example given: horn length in crossed cattle appearing late in life due to the male element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversion when turned wild (claim and evidential standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The often-stated claim that domestic varieties, when run wild, gradually revert to their aboriginal stocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove this decisively one would need appropriate experiments: release a single variety into a new home (to avoid intercrossing) and observe under unchanged conditions for many generations. Darwin finds no solid evidence that domestic varieties generally lose acquired characters under unchanged conditions when kept in a considerable body (where free intercrossing occurs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary evidence to infer loss of acquired characters
rubrics_metrics.description: To deduce that domestic varieties cannot inform species origins, one must show they have a strong tendency to lose acquired characters while kept under unchanged conditions and in a large interbreeding body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin finds 'not a shadow of evidence' for such a general tendency; absence of this evidence means domestic races remain informative about species-change under selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare uniformity: domestic races vs true species
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic races of the same species generally show less uniformity of character than true species closely allied in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use degree of uniformity as a comparative criterion; domestic races may also show extreme, localized differences but still be less uniform overall than natural species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monstrous (extreme) character in domestic races
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic races often have a somewhat monstrous character: differing only slightly in many respects but exhibiting an extreme change in some single part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pattern (extreme change in one part) is common among domesticated forms and can be used to explain why breeders and some naturalists mistake varieties for distinct species; selection can accumulate small changes producing such extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence/absence of generic-value characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that domestic races do not differ from each other in characters of generic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin disputes the absolute correctness of this claim and notes that valuations of 'generic' characters are empirical and vary among naturalists; thus generic-character differences are not a decisive criterion here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fertility of hybrids among domestic breeds
rubrics_metrics.description: Hybrids (mongrels) from between all the domestic breeds of pigeons are perfectly fertile (according to Darwin's observations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfect fertility among very distinct domestic forms is unusual between clearly distinct wild species; this fertility supports descent from a single species. Darwin notes the rarity of perfectly fertile hybrids between clearly distinct species, so fertility of breeds is strong evidence of common origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improbability of multiple wild prototypes (population and survival criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inference that the many distinct domestic breeds could not each have descended from separate wild species given lack of wild prototypes, absence of feral forms, and improbability of extinction of many similar wild species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments include: few rock-pigeon-like wild species exist; extermination of numerous rock-pigeon-like species is unlikely; transported breeds have not become feral in native lands; domestication of many wild species to prolific breeding under confinement in ancient times is improbable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reappearance of ancestral characters in crosses (reversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: When distinct breeds are crossed, characters of the presumed ancestral wild stock (e.g., rock-pigeon coloration and markings) may suddenly reappear in mongrel offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin uses these reappearance phenomena as evidence of reversion to ancestral characters and thus of common ancestry. Example: crosses between white fantails and black barbs produced grandchildren with rock-pigeon blue colour, white rump, wing-bars, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of crossing to produce extreme new breeds
rubrics_metrics.description: Crossing produces first-generation offspring fairly uniform, but when mongrels are interbred for several generations they become highly variable and it is extremely difficult or hopeless to produce a stable, intermediate permanent breed between two very distinct breeds solely by crossing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical observation (Sir J. Sebright's experiments, pigeon crosses) indicates crossing alone rarely yields stable intermediate races without prolonged, careful selection; selecting mongrels with desired traits is required but often fails to produce permanent races.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of morphological variability within breeds
rubrics_metrics.description: A wide range of anatomical and physiological traits vary among breeds: beak shape, skull structure, wattle, eyelid length, nostril orifice size, crop development, oil-gland presence, number of tail and wing feathers, vertebrae counts, ribs and processes, sternum apertures, wing/tail/body proportions, leg and foot proportions, toe scutellæ, down state, egg shape and size, flight manner, voice, disposition, sexual dimorphism degree, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin lists these variable traits in pigeons to show how extreme and many-sided variation within a single domestic lineage can be, supporting the feasibility of producing very different breeds from one wild species through selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and geographic evidence for long-term selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Records from antiquity (Egyptian dynasties, Roman times, Indian courts, Dutch breeders) showing long cultivation, high value, and pedigreed breeding of pigeons and other domestic animals indicate long-term human selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use antiquity and wide geographic cultivation as evidence that selection has had many generations to act, explaining the large amount of variation seen among breeds; presence of old records argues against multiple, recent wild origins for each breed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial selection (accumulative selection) as explanatory mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Man's power of accumulative selection: nature supplies successive variations; man accumulates those useful to him in certain directions to make useful breeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin emphasizes both methodical (intentional) selection and unconscious selection. Examples: breeders modifying cattle and sheep within a lifetime, commercial merino-breeding in Saxony, selective marking and culling, and horticulturists' rapid improvements. Selection explains adaptation of domestic races to human use or fancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconscious selection and 'roguing' in seed-raising
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconscious selection results because everyone tries to possess and breed from the best individuals; in horticulture seed-raisers 'pull up the rogues' that deviate from standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ubiquitous, non-deliberate selection complements methodical selection and contributes substantially to the formation of domestic races over generations; recognition of both forms is necessary when evaluating breed origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise and practicability of selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective selection demands exceptional accuracy of eye, sound judgment, years of study, perseverance, and sometimes trade-like practice; not everyone can be an eminent breeder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites breeders' testimony and practices (e.g., Sir John Sebright, Youatt, Lord Somerville) to argue that realistic appraisal of breeding outcomes must account for breeder skill; this supports the plausibility of profound change by human selection when practiced systematically.
